intro: These are the ways the platform must be able to grow, each told as a situation, with the person who does the growing, what they should need to touch, and what must stay untouched; they say what is needed, never how to build it. The owner named two kinds of game extension, and each case says which it is, or that it is neither: a case that fits the engine to a venue or a production, or a developer's addition that gives no new game mechanic (support for a program, a content tool or other hardware). In the first kind a game's own maker builds a new mechanic inside the game from what the engine can already do: a new action for the players, or a new way the game responds to a trigger the engine already has. In the second kind a developer extends the engine so that any game can use a response it cannot give yet. The owner's wording is tentative ('should probably', 'probably'), and the cases keep it so. How an extension for all games relates to the engine's main release, and which piece each kind changes (the pack, the engine's code, an added outside service), are the owner's open questions. The independent panel designs against them beside the ten promises and the quality targets, and every case not marked proposed rests on a decision the owner has already made or a roadmap section the owner ratified. 'The published protocol' here is the owner's name for one versioned definition of everything that crosses the engine's edge: what a device may ask, what the engine answers, what it tells screens, and the files that carry a game or a night (the pack, the venue profile, the night's record, the media list). Every program's code is generated from it or checked against it. It is settled, and it is designed in an early design round.

cases.title: A whole second game, as a pack
cases.case: A designer who did not build ALN makes a whole second game: its tokens and their texts, its modes, scoring, groups, cues, clock, words and look. They publish it, and that night the whole kit plays it: the engine scores by it, the TV shows its words, every tablet and scanner holds the same copy, and the GM can see at a glance that they match. The toy game kept beside ALN is the standing test that this works for a game that is not ALN.
cases.throughWhat: A pack, written in the design tool and published through the engine's own check that refuses a broken pack; a media bundle for the files the pack names.
cases.mustNotNeed: The engine's code, its settings files, new firmware for the hardware scanner, ALN's pack, or any word of ALN's inside the engine.
cases.when: now for the pack; checking the media against the pack in the preview block; the media bundle and its upload later (the content tooling block)
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's final outcome and its design-iteration loop; the glossary's entry on the toy game's pack; your decision "Design for the long term, beyond ALN")
cases.why: The platform exists so that a game is data the engine plays, and ALN is one pack among others.

cases.title: Change one value between shows and play it
cases.case: Between two shows the designer changes one value, say a token's rating or a group's bonus, applies it to the running engine, and plays a round to feel the change, all within minutes. A game in progress never receives the change: the engine applies it only at a moment its lifecycle allows, between games, or refuses and says why. Every copy of the pack in the kit is told, and the GM sees which version each device runs.
cases.throughWhat: The pack, edited as a draft in the design tool and published; the engine applies the change only between games, or refuses and says why.
cases.mustNotNeed: A restart of the engine, a code or settings change, a rebuild of the tablet or phone app, or any touch on a running game's records.
cases.when: a planned block: the preview block (the rules editor and applying a change while the engine runs are one deliverable)
promises: The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
Each lifecycle button does exactly what its name says
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's design-iteration loop and the roadmap's row for deferred work on applying a change while the engine runs; your decision "Standalone games: declared, never mixed" keeps it on the list every design choice must serve)
cases.why: Making games playable without code or settings files is the point of the engine work, and speed is what makes the loop usable.

cases.title: A third way to turn in a token
cases.case: A designer adds a third thing a team can do with a token, for example 'donate it to the archive': the token is used up, no money moves, and the result lands on the evidence screen. They describe the new mode by its flags, how it scores, whether it uses the token up, where its result shows, and name it on screen in their own words. The engine reads the flags and never the mode's name, so ALN's two modes and this third one are the same kind of thing to it.
cases.throughWhat: The pack's list of modes, and the pack's strings that name the mode on screen.
cases.mustNotNeed: The engine's code, the screens' code, or any change to another game's pack.
cases.when: now
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
One game, the same on every screen
cases.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entry on the ways a team can turn in a token, each declared in the pack; the roadmap's rule that the engine holds no opinion)
cases.why: The engine holds no opinion about game design, so a way of turning in a token is a pack value, not engine code.

cases.title: A new scoring model added once
cases.case: A game needs a way of scoring the engine has never had, for example a score read off a graph of connected tokens instead of a table of values. A developer adds it once as a generic model with its own parameters. A designer selects the model in their pack and tunes its parameters like any other pack value. A pack that asks for a model the engine lacks is refused when published, with the model named, instead of running with the wrong rules.
cases.throughWhat: A module of the engine's own rules library, selected by the pack by name and listed among the abilities the pack requires; the parameters in the pack.
cases.mustNotNeed: ALN's pack or ALN's rules, the tablet's screens, the hardware scanner's firmware, or a fork of the engine for that game.
cases.when: later (the roadmap's second game's modules block)
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
One game, the same on every screen
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's second game's modules block; the glossary's entries on the abilities a pack requires and on the rules the engine and a standalone tablet share; the owner's decision 'Two kinds of game extension', which places a new scoring model, an ability the engine lacks, in its second kind as the agent running the pass reads it; how it relates to the engine's main release is the owner's open question)
cases.why: The rules are written once and run by the engine and by a standalone tablet alike, so a new model is one addition, not two.

cases.title: Adding tokens and their media files
cases.case: A designer adds twenty tokens with new texts, pictures, sounds and three videos. The texts and the names of the files go into the pack; the files themselves go into the media bundle through the design tool. Before the show, a check says whether every file the pack names is on the show machine, by a fingerprint of its content. The hardware scanners fetch the new pictures and sounds by themselves at their next start.
cases.throughWhat: The pack (tokens, texts, file names with fingerprints) and the media bundle, uploaded through the design tool and moved as one to the show machine.
cases.mustNotNeed: Media files inside the pack's repository, files copied by hand into folders on the show machine, engine code, or a visit to each hardware scanner.
cases.when: now for the pack's content; a planned block, the preview block, for checking the bundle against the pack's list; later (the roadmap's content tooling block) for the upload experience
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's media model and the roadmap's row for deferred work on media reference checking; the glossary's entries on carrying the pack's media files and on the channel the hardware scanner fetches its files on)
cases.why: The pack stays small and names its media; the files travel in a bundle that can be checked and moved between machines.

cases.title: A cue names roles, the venue binds them
cases.case: A designer adds a cue: at the ninety-minute mark the lights go to a 'police arrival' look, a siren plays and the music turns down. They name the look by its role in the show. Which real lamp and which scene make that look is the venue technician's business, bound per venue. The designer also marks whether the lights are needed. In a venue with no lights tonight, marked 'skip it', the cue's lighting shows as not installed tonight, grey, and the siren still plays; marked 'block the show', the preflight says no-go and the game does not start without the typed override.
cases.throughWhat: The pack's cues, naming lighting roles, sound files and display channels; the venue profile binds each name to an instrument.
cases.mustNotNeed: A venue's scene ids or speaker names inside the pack, engine code, or a change to the GM's screens.
cases.when: now for cues that name roles; the last speaker name leaves the pack in the preview block, and the venue scene ids kept as lighting fallbacks leave it in the depth-and-close block
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
The game fits the venue it is in tonight
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
cases.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entries on cues and on how each light the pack names is bound to a real light, with a fallback; the roadmap's row for deferred work on the last speaker name in pack content)
cases.why: Venue details never enter the pack, so one game's cues play in any room the pack's names can be bound to.

cases.title: Each game's own words, colours and labels
cases.case: One game calls its score-holders 'Accounts', another 'Crews'; one shows star ratings, another hides them; each has its own colours and its own award message. The designer sets these in the pack, and the GM's tablet, the TV and the phones all use them, with the same words in the editor as at the show. The engine's own fallback words appear only when a pack declares none.
cases.throughWhat: The pack's strings file, its theme file and its score-holder label.
cases.mustNotNeed: Engine code, the screens' code, or a rebuild of the tablet or phone apps.
cases.when: now (built); the strings and theme editor, showing the result on a real device: a planned block, the depth-and-close block
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
cases.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entries on the pack's strings file, its theme file and the word for a score-holder; roadmap, the depth-and-close block)
cases.why: Even the word for a score-holder comes from the pack, so no screen carries ALN's vocabulary.

cases.title: A game divided into acts
cases.case: A designer divides the game into acts. A cue fires two minutes into act two, and the GM moves the game from act to act with one button when the room is ready, not by the clock alone. The acts and the timings are the designer's; the button is the engine's, and what it does at pause, end and reset is defined.
cases.throughWhat: The pack's clock and phases block, and cues timed relative to a phase.
cases.mustNotNeed: Engine code or a change to the GM's screens for a new set of acts.
cases.when: the GM scanner redesign carries it: its design opens in the preview block, and its build is priced and slotted by its own planning session; no block delivers it yet
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
Each lifecycle button does exactly what its name says
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's row for deferred work on the GM scanner redesign; the promise 'One game, the same on every screen', whose needs name the phase as a new fact the GM writes)
cases.why: The phase is a fact the GM writes, so it needs a decider, a saved home and a defined fate at every lifecycle moment, like any other game fact.

cases.title: Configuring screens, and a new kind of screen
cases.who: designer; developer for a new kind of screen
cases.case: A designer turns the scoreboard off for a game with no public score, or changes how fast the evidence pages turn, in the pack. A game that needs a new kind of public screen, say a constellation of nodes and edges, gets it as code a developer adds once that draws the new kind of screen; the pack selects it and themes it. A screen receives only what it may show: hidden facts are filtered before they leave the engine, never on the screen itself.
cases.throughWhat: The pack's screen settings for the built-in screens; for a new kind of screen, the code that draws it, added once at the place a new kind of screen plugs in, selected by the pack and listed among the abilities it requires.
cases.mustNotNeed: The engine's core code or ALN's scoreboard page for a new screen kind; no screen's own code to keep hidden facts hidden.
cases.when: now for selecting and configuring the built-in screens; later for the constellation screen (the second game's modules); a general way to add new kinds of screen has no slot yet
promises: One game, the same on every screen
Each person sees their part and can do only their part
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
cases.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entry on kinds of screen; the roadmap's second game's modules block and the roadmap's row for deferred work on new kinds of screen defined by the pack, which keeps the general case as room left beyond the constellation screen)
cases.why: Packs can configure the three built-in screens today but cannot define new ones; the second game's constellation screen is the first new kind, and the only one with a slot.

cases.title: Players' own phones and two-tap actions
cases.who: designer; developer for each device kind's support
cases.case: A game lets players use their own phones: tap a token, a web page opens, no account, no login, no app. The same game asks for a two-tap action: a player taps their own token, then another player's, and something happens between them. The designer declares which device kinds its players use, what each may do, and the two-tap action's rules, in the pack. The phone and the hardware scanner both perform the action, each in its own way on its own screen. A developer builds each device kind's support once, as platform work, never per game. How many phones one kit carries at once is a production's setting, measured before the first phone is admitted, under the quality target "[[qt:QT34]]".
cases.throughWhat: The pack (device classes, what each may do, the multi-tap actions); the published protocol; everything the designer iterates on reaches the device as pack data, never firmware.
cases.mustNotNeed: New firmware for each game, a second hand-written copy of the rules inside a device, player accounts or logins, or a change to another game's pack.
cases.when: later (the roadmap's players' phones block; the roadmap's row for deferred work on the kit's network name and certificate)
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
Each person sees their part and can do only their part
The game fits the venue it is in tonight
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's players' phones block, its rules on identity and player data and its platform parity rule; your decision "Standalone games: declared, never mixed" keeps phones on the list every design choice must serve)
cases.why: Phones and hardware scanners must stay equal in what they can drive, and everything a designer iterates on must be pack data, never firmware.

cases.title: Who may do what on which device
cases.case: One game wants players named: a typed name on their own phone, or a scanned band at a shared station. Another wants nobody named. A third lets a shared station make a transaction that only a GM may make today. The designer sets this per game: which device classes exist, what each may do, whether a person is ever identified. In every game, starting, pausing and ending the game, show control and score changes stay with staff who log in, such as the GM.
cases.throughWhat: The pack (device classes, what each may do, the identification moment); the pack says what each kind of device may do, within the limit that starting, pausing and ending the game, show control and score changes stay with staff who log in, such as the GM.
cases.mustNotNeed: Player accounts or logins, an engine default about naming people, a change to the engine's code, or any loosening of the limit that keeps starting, pausing and ending the game, show control and score changes with staff who log in.
cases.when: now for the staff-only limit; later (the roadmap's players' phones block, the access model that grants each right by function) for pack-assigned rights per device class
promises: Each person sees their part and can do only their part
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's rules on identity and player data and its rule that the engine holds no opinion; the glossary's entries on the staff-only limit and on the GM scanner versus the player scanner)
cases.why: Who may do what on which device is game design, and the engine holds no opinion about game design; only the staff-only limit is engine law.

cases.title: A game with no show machine
cases.who: designer declares it; the GMs run it, and whether player scanners alone may is the owner's open question on the shapes
cases.kind: neither: fitting the engine to a venue or a production
cases.case: A game runs where a network connection is not feasible, or where other logistics make it better to use only GM scanners, player scanners (phone or hardware), or both. The designer declares the game standalone. Each device works alone: the tablet says 'standalone', never 'disconnected', runs the same rules the engine would, and its record names the pack version it played. No game mixes devices on an engine with devices working alone. The hardware scanner plays the game as the phone's scanner does; today it cannot, which is a parity gap to close. Which effects a standalone game may use, exposed evidence and video among them, is the owner's question 'What a standalone game gives up, and what it keeps'; what a screen draws for an exposure or a video token with no engine, under that rule, is a default the agent running the pass proposes and the owner can overrule. Where the declaration lives (the venue profile, the pack, the game's record or each device) is a question for the design rounds. Which shapes of standalone game the engine supports (GM scanners, player scanners or both, and how many GM tablets) is the owner's open question.
cases.throughWhat: A declaration held in the venue profile, the pack, the game's record or each device (the design rounds choose where), read by every device; the same rules module on the tablet.
cases.mustNotNeed: An engine, venue equipment, a second hand-kept copy of the rules on the tablet, or any engine code.
cases.when: the design must allow it now; nothing builds it yet, and where the declaration lives is a design-rounds question
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
One game, the same on every screen
Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
cases.status: settled by the owner (the owner's decision 'Standalone games: declared, never mixed', with its purpose stated 2026-11-02; the owner's words 'player scanners (phone or hardware)' settle the hardware scanner's reading); open: where the declaration lives, and which shapes of standalone game the engine supports
cases.why: A whole game with no engine is on the list every design choice must serve, and today nothing in the pack can say so.

cases.title: A new venue is a new profile
cases.kind: neither: fitting the engine to a venue or a production
cases.case: The kit goes to a new venue. The technician reads the pack's tech rider, fills in a profile of what the room has tonight (which speakers, which lights, which network, how many stations and how many extra scoreboard screens), binds each of the pack's names to a real instrument on one page, and runs one preflight that says go or no-go. Each line says what it checked and whether it checked paper or the live room. Equipment left at home shows as not installed tonight, grey, never red. A second venue is a second profile; the pack is the same.
cases.throughWhat: A venue profile, edited in the venue technician's tool, with its bindings page, its profile manager and the preflight; the tech rider derived from the pack.
cases.mustNotNeed: The pack, the engine's code, kit-unique names inside code, or a developer.
cases.when: now for the profile and the hand-run checklist; the one-button preflight with paper or live on every line is hardening work rebuilt inside the architecture pass (today only a minimal check exists); a planned block, the depth-and-close block, for the bindings page and the profile manager; later (the roadmap's row for deferred work on the planning view) for 'what does bringing hardware X unlock'
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's final outcome; the glossary's entries on the venue technician, the preflight, paper versus live checks, the hand-off from designer to venue technician to GM, and the tech rider; your decision "Promises, qualities, moments, venue technician", which names the venue technician)
cases.why: Everything specific to a venue lives in its profile, so fitting a game to a room is the technician's work alone.

cases.title: Rehearsing the whole show on stand-ins
cases.kind: neither: fitting the engine to a venue or a production
cases.case: On a laptop with no lights, speakers or TV, or on the show machine between games (where it runs is an open question), the designer rehearses the whole show: every player action performed in its simulated form, the show reacting for real on software stand-ins. The profile for this is generated from the pack's own needs so that every need is met; every verdict on screen says 'paper', never 'live'. The live engine, its programs and its records are untouched, and nothing the trial copy issues is accepted by the live one.
cases.throughWhat: A venue profile whose bindings point at software stand-ins, generated from the pack; a separate trial copy of the engine with its own files, ports and settings.
cases.mustNotNeed: A change to the pack, the live engine's programs or records, or any hardware.
cases.when: a planned block: the preview block
promises: The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
cases.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entries on running a show on software stand-ins and on rehearsing it without the venue; roadmap, the preview block; your decision "Standalone games: declared, never mixed" keeps the trial copy on the list every design choice must serve)
cases.why: A simulation is an ordinary profile bound to stand-ins, so rehearsing changes nothing in the pack and reaches nothing live.

cases.title: A different lighting system or video player
cases.who: developer adds the support; the venue technician says in the profile what the room has tonight
cases.kind: neither: a developer's addition that is no game mechanic
cases.case: A kit uses a different lighting system, or the team replaces the video player. A developer adds the support once, for every kit; it is not a new game mechanic, so it is neither of the owner's two kinds of game extension. The venue technician then says in the profile what the room has tonight. The pack, the cues, the GM's screens and the support for the other programs do not change. The new program has a software stand-in for tests and rehearsal. A setting says whether the engine starts the program itself or uses one already running, and the program watcher restarts it like any other.
cases.throughWhat: Support for the program, added once inside the engine, with its software stand-in; the setting that says whether the engine starts each program or uses one already running (where that setting lives, in the venue profile or in a settings file on the machine, is open for the design rounds).
cases.mustNotNeed: The pack, any cue, the GM's screens, the support for the other programs, the engine's rules, or the lifecycle.
cases.when: the design must allow it now; how the engine reaches its programs is decided in the design rounds; the program watcher and the start-or-use setting are hardening work rebuilt inside the architecture pass, and where that setting lives is open
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
cases.status: settled by the owner for the program watcher (the glossary's entry on the program watcher, ratified 2026-09-04); the need itself rests on the promise 'The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked', the glossary's entry on running a show on software stand-ins and the owner's decision 'The engine is hardware-flexible; the roadmap sets the bounds', since a kit's lights and players are part of its hardware; the owner's decision 'Two kinds of game extension' says what this case is not; open for the design rounds: how the engine reaches its programs, and where the start-or-use setting lives
cases.why: A kit may bring different lights or a different video player than ours, and the program behind a cue must be replaceable without touching the game or the GM's screens.

cases.title: A second production takes the platform
cases.kind: neither: fitting the engine to a venue or a production
cases.case: A second production takes the platform: another operator with their own kit, their own venue profiles and a library of installed packs, picking one per event. Their kit has its own network name and its own machine; two kits in one building never confuse each other's devices. Nothing in the engine assumes one kit, one pack or one production. They read what is fixed and what they may set (the case 'Another production adopts the engine for its venue and hardware'), then install the engine and go.
cases.throughWhat: Their own venue profiles and installed packs; the engine's per-kit settings (its network name, one written list of what the machine should carry); their own copy of the engine with its own files, ports and settings.
cases.mustNotNeed: Engine code, a kit-unique name inside code, our pack, our venue profile, or our live machine.
cases.when: later (the roadmap's operations era and release block, fleet growth and multi-game kits); what keeps it cheap is built now (the roadmap's rule on growth without corners): each pack and profile picked by name, no kit's own names inside the engine's code, a network name per kit, media that moves between machines
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's final outcome, its rule on growth without corners and its operations era and release block; the owner's decision 'The engine says what is fixed and what each production sets')
cases.why: The business plans one kit, but every design must keep a second one cheap to start later.

cases.title: A new engine version by swapping machines
cases.kind: neither: fitting the engine to a venue or a production
cases.case: A new engine version is ready. The owner builds a second machine, checks that it carries everything on one written list of what it should carry (engine version, tablet and phone apps, pack version, media by fingerprint, venue profile), rehearses on it, and swaps it in between events by replugging. If the night goes wrong, replugging the old machine brings everything back as it was. After the swap, packs may change at any time by publishing; the engine changes only between events.
cases.throughWhat: One written list of what the machine should carry, so the owner can see that a machine carries everything on that list before it goes out; the swap of machines; the pack channel for pack updates.
cases.mustNotNeed: An upgrade of the live machine in place, files copied by hand, a change to the pack for the new engine version, or a developer at the venue.
cases.when: now for the swap (the method is ratified; the between-events rule takes over after the first swap); the check that a machine carries everything on its written list is new work
promises: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
Each lifecycle button does exactly what its name says
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's method for swapping in the new machine and its operations era and release block, steady-state releases; your stated goal of the work, 2026-10-30)
cases.why: The owner alone sends a version to the venue, and must be able to take it back by moving a plug.

cases.title: A different content tool feeds the same pack
cases.who: developer writes the adapter; the designer uses it
cases.kind: neither: a developer's addition that is no game mechanic
cases.case: A designer writes their game's content in a different tool, or in the platform's own content database once it exists: tokens and characters, timeline, puzzles and lore. A developer writes one source adapter for that tool; it feeds the same pack through the same check that refuses a broken pack. The scanners, the engine and the night's record never notice where the content came from, and the game's own after-game telling reads the record, not the content tool.
cases.throughWhat: A source adapter behind a published interface for content sources; the pack it produces is the ordinary pack.
cases.mustNotNeed: The engine's code, the pack's formats, the check at publish, the scanners, or the after-game telling.
cases.when: later (the roadmap's content tooling block; the roadmap's row for deferred work on the source adapter)
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's content tooling block and the roadmap's row for deferred work on the source adapter; the glossary's entry on the source adapter)
cases.why: Content tooling is a convenience, never a dependency: the pack is the one source every tool feeds, and Notion is only its first source.

cases.title: The director tells the night from the record
cases.who: director; the game's own developer builds the telling
cases.kind: neither: fitting the engine to a venue or a production
cases.case: The game ends. The engine writes one record of the night: the facts it decided, with the roster, the GM's notes, the accusation and the photos captured during play, the pack the game ran and the texts the players saw. ALN's Director Console, a separate program on the director's computer, reads that record, and the director writes the players' story from it, quoting what they held, with no retyping and no reading of Notion. The record is shaped so that a game's telling can later run inside the engine's Review stage. What reaches the players afterwards, and their emails, stay the game's business outside the engine.
cases.throughWhat: The night's record, a published file format read from outside the engine; later, if the owner chooses, a module of the game's own inside the Review stage.
cases.mustNotNeed: The engine's code, the GM tablet's report pasted and parsed back into lists, Notion, players' emails or consent inside the engine, or the live machine.
cases.when: a planned block: the capture block (writing the record when the game ends); later (the roadmap's row for deferred work on the report pipeline's move) for the console reading it, owner-paced
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
cases.status: settled by the owner (your decision "The night's record and the after-game article"; the roadmap's row for deferred work on the report pipeline's move; the glossary's entry on the Review stage, where the night is told afterwards)
cases.why: The platform owns the record, the intake and the hand-over to the game; the game owns the telling, and it must be able to tell from what was captured, not reconstructed.

cases.title: The owner's second game needs new modules
cases.who: developer builds the modules; the designer (the owner) tunes the game
cases.case: The owner's second game needs four things the engine has never had: two-tap actions between players' objects, hidden per-player and per-token state that spreads on contact, a score read off a graph, and a constellation screen. A developer builds each as a generic module with pack-supplied parameters. The owner then finishes the game's design at his own pace with no further engineering, tuning spread rates and seeds like any other pack values and playtesting them through the edit, apply, play loop. A second toy game proves the modules the way the first toy game proves the engine. The game needs an engine by nature and its pack says so. A hidden fact reaches only its owner's screen.
cases.throughWhat: Generic modules of the engine's own (the rules, multi-tap player actions, and the place a new kind of screen plugs in), each an ability the pack requires and selects by name; the game's values in its pack.
cases.mustNotNeed: A fork of the engine for that game, code with the game's name in it, ALN's pack or ALN's screens, or a screen that filters hidden facts itself.
cases.when: later (the roadmap's second game's modules block; the game's design track is open now, owner-paced)
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
One game, the same on every screen
Each person sees their part and can do only their part
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's second game's modules block and the roadmap's row for deferred work on new kinds of screen defined by the pack)
cases.why: The platform delivers all the technology the second game needs, so its design finishes without software engineering, and a third game can reuse the same modules.

cases.title: A stranger extends the platform from the guide
cases.case: A stranger downloads the platform, stands it up from the guide, opens the toy game and builds something new: support for a device, support for a program the engine drives, a scoring model or a content source. They work from the published protocol and the toy game as a worked example, and send their change back with the developer's tests, which show that the show still runs for both games. How their change joins the engine's main release is the owner's open question. They never see our secrets, our pack or our venue, and the privacy defaults every operator inherits are written down for them.
cases.throughWhat: The published protocol (what devices may ask, what the engine answers and tells screens, the pack, the venue profile, the night's record, the media list); the places a developer adds a device, a program, a scoring model or a content source; the human-facing designer and operator guides; the toy game; a license.
cases.mustNotNeed: Private knowledge of the team, our pack, our venue profile, our live machine, or a committed password or token in the repository.
cases.when: later (the roadmap's release block, and its readiness state adoptable); the committed secrets rotate before the first outsider touches the system
promises: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
Each person sees their part and can do only their part
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's final outcome, its readiness states, adoptable and previewable, and its release block; the owner's decision 'The engine says what is fixed and what each production sets': the written list of what is fixed is part of what the stranger stands the platform up from)
cases.why: The end goal is an open-source show platform that non-technical designers can use and technical people can extend.

cases.title: The pack says what a scan causes
cases.case: A designer declares what a scan causes: for example, that a GM's scan of a token plays that token's video, or that a player's scan does nothing on the TV. Today only a player's scan can trigger a video, a rule of ALN's built into the engine; a game played only on GM tablets reaches video through one standing cue per token, which is pack content and works today.
cases.throughWhat: The pack: what each kind of scan triggers, written beside the token or the mode.
cases.mustNotNeed: Engine code, a change to the scanners, or a standing cue per token once the declaration exists.
cases.when: later, with multi-tap player actions (the players' phones block); until then, one standing cue per token
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's rule that the engine holds no opinion and the roadmap's row for deferred work on GM-scan video cueing; the glossary's entry on the resting video versus a video a game event plays; the owner's decision 'Two kinds of game extension': what a scan causes is a mechanic made inside the game, and the owner's own example, players changing the lighting by scanning tokens, rests on it)
cases.why: The engine holds no opinion about game design, so which scan triggers which consequence is a pack value, not an engine rule keyed to one kind of scanner.

cases.title: A different installed game each night
cases.kind: neither: fitting the engine to a venue or a production
cases.case: Our own kit runs a different installed game per event: ALN on Friday, another game on Saturday. The operator picks the installed pack for the night, and the engine, the TV, the tablets and the scanners play it, without copying files or changing code. Both games stay installed; neither is touched by the other's night.
cases.throughWhat: An installed pack picked by name: at startup by path or id today; a selection page later.
cases.mustNotNeed: Engine code, a settings change by hand, files copied in and out, or a second machine per game.
cases.when: now, by picking the pack at startup by path or id; a selection page later (the roadmap's operations era and release block, multi-game kits)
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
The game fits the venue it is in tonight
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's final outcome, the interim state: one kit and a growing library of its own games; its operations era and release block, multi-game kits, 'a real requirement'; its rule on growth without corners)
cases.why: The business is one production with many games on one kit, so switching games is the operator's choice for the night, never work for a developer.

cases.title: The owner sets how long records are kept
cases.kind: neither: fitting the engine to a venue or a production
cases.case: The owner decides, per game, how long old game records (the night's record, the photos, the scans) are kept, and nothing a game captured leaves the kit unless the owner moves it. A game that names players, through an identification moment the designer chose, inherits the same rules. A future operator inherits them too, written down.
cases.throughWhat: A per-game setting for how long records are kept; the kit as the only home of game data unless the owner moves it.
cases.mustNotNeed: Engine code, an account for any player, any place for game data off the kit that the owner did not choose, or a default the engine sets for every game.
cases.when: the design must allow it now; these are the privacy defaults every operator inherits
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
Each person sees their part and can do only their part
cases.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's rules on identity and player data, that game data stays on the kit and that how long it is kept is your decision per game: the privacy defaults every future operator inherits)
cases.why: Game data stays on the kit and its keeping is the owner's call per game; a platform other operators take up must carry those defaults with it.

cases.title: Players change the room's lighting by scanning tokens
cases.case: A designer wants the players to change the room's lighting by scanning different tokens on a player scanner. The engine can already read a player's scan and light a named look, so the designer combines the two inside the game, through the case 'The pack says what a scan causes': this token's scan triggers that look. In the owner's tentative words this 'should probably' be the game's own maker's work, with no developer; how far the maker may go with no developer is the owner's question 'What a game's maker may build inside the pack'. In the long term the designer may share the mechanic with other game makers for their games, a possibility the owner named, not a plan.
cases.throughWhat: The pack: what a scan causes (the case 'The pack says what a scan causes'), naming a lighting look by its role; the venue profile binds the look to the room's lights.
cases.mustNotNeed: Engine code, new firmware, or a change to another game's pack; probably no developer, as the owner's words have it.
cases.when: later, once the pack says what a scan causes (the players' phones block); until then, one standing cue per token
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
cases.status: settled by the owner on the kind (the owner's decision 'Two kinds of game extension', with this as the owner's own example of a mechanic made inside a game; the roadmap's rule that the engine holds no opinion); open for the owner: how far the game's maker may go with no developer (the question 'What a game's maker may build inside the pack')
cases.why: A mechanic built from what the engine already does should probably be the game maker's own work, in the owner's words, so the engine's abilities should combine inside the game without a developer.

cases.title: Audio in several rooms, added once for every game
cases.case: A venue has several rooms. A developer adds a service such as Snapcast so that different areas get different soundtracks, and the GMs can play a sound cue on every speaker or on chosen speakers (areas or rooms of the game space). The ability is added once, and any game can then use it. Which piece the addition changes (the engine's code, an added outside service, the pack), and so how a pack asks for areas and a venue profile binds them to real speakers, is the owner's open question. ALN's pack and the toy game's pack run as before, and a pack that needs the ability on an engine without it is refused at the desk with the ability named.
cases.throughWhat: The places the owner's open question settles (the engine's code, an added outside service, the pack), with a software stand-in for tests; the ability listed among those a pack may require.
cases.mustNotNeed: A fork of the engine, a change to packs that do not use areas, or a change to the GM's screens for games that do not.
cases.when: the design must leave room for it now; no block delivers it
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
The game fits the venue it is in tonight
A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
cases.status: settled by the owner on the kind (the owner's decision 'Two kinds of game extension', with this as the owner's own example of extending the engine for all games); open for the owner: how such an extension relates to the engine's main release, and which piece it changes (the engine's code, an added outside service, the pack)
cases.why: A response the engine cannot give yet is a developer's work for every game, so the engine needs a place where a new service plugs in and a way for a pack to say it needs it.

cases.title: Another production adopts the engine for its venue and hardware
cases.who: operator of another production, with their venue technician
cases.kind: neither: fitting the engine to a venue or a production
cases.case: Another production, with a different game, venue and hardware, takes up the engine. Before they buy or build anything, they find in one place which requirements are fixed (the hardware the engine requires, the network it needs, the limits it states) and which the engine lets them choose (their kit's devices and phones, their set-up time, how long they keep records, their machine's limits). They fit the engine to their venue from that list and the guide alone, and never read the code to learn what is fixed. ALN is the first production: one game, one venue, the hardware the owner bought.
cases.throughWhat: One written list of fixed requirements and stated limits, kept with the guide; the venue profile and the production's own settings for everything else.
cases.mustNotNeed: A developer, engine code, ALN's pack or profile, or a reading of the code.
cases.when: the design must allow it now: every number in the quality targets is sorted as the engine's, a production's or a technical default; when the written list ships is for the build plan
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
cases.status: settled by the owner (the owner's decision 'The engine says what is fixed and what each production sets')
cases.why: In the owner's words: 'what they need to know is what is a fixes requirement vs what affordances the engine allows in order for them to fit its use into their needs and venue realities.'

cases.title: A different show machine or scanner hardware
cases.who: developer adds the support; the roadmap says whether now
cases.kind: neither: a developer's addition that is no game mechanic
cases.case: A production runs the engine on a different show machine than a Raspberry Pi, or brings a different hardware scanner. A different show machine or scanner board can be supported later without changing the packs, the profiles, the game rules or the GM's screens. Whether the current roadmap builds that support now, or names the Raspberry Pi and today's scanner as specific hardware requirements for now, is the bound the roadmap sets.
cases.throughWhat: The places the engine leaves for hardware support: the show machine's set-up, each device kind's support through the published protocol, and a software stand-in for each; the written list of what is fixed, which names the hardware the current roadmap requires.
cases.mustNotNeed: A fork of the engine, a change to packs, profiles or the game rules, or a change to the GM's screens.
cases.when: the architecture must allow it now; which hardware the current roadmap supports, and where it names specific requirements, is open for the design rounds and the build plan
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
cases.status: settled by the owner on the direction (the owner's decision 'The engine is hardware-flexible; the roadmap sets the bounds'); open: where the current roadmap draws the line
cases.why: In the owner's words: 'the point of the engine in its mature form is that it is flexible meaning that we should build the fundamental architecture to allow flexibility with the hardware down the line.'
